title: Open Problem: polytime $f(\mathrm{OPT})$-approximation for largest complete minor
statement_text: It is open whether finding the size of a largest complete minor admits a polynomial-time $f(\mathrm{OPT})$-approximation algorithm.
context_text: The problem takes a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and asks for the largest $t$ (denoted $\mathrm{OPT}$) such that $K_t$ is a minor of $G$. A polynomial-time $f(\mathrm{OPT})$-approximation algorithm would, for some function $f$ independent of $n$, output in polynomial time a value within a factor $f(\mathrm{OPT})$ of the optimum (for instance, finding a $K_t$ minor or certifying that there is no $K_{f(t)}$ minor). Testing for a fixed $K_t$ minor is fixed-parameter tractable (Robertson–Seymour, time $f(t)n^3$; Korhonen, Pilipczuk and Stamoulis, $f(t)n^{1+o(1)}$), but computing the largest complete minor is NP-hard (Eppstein), has no PTAS unless P $=$ NP (Wahlén), and the best known polynomial-time approximation factor is $O(\sqrt n)$ (Alon, Lingas and Wahlén). The paper studies the analogue for ordered graphs (graphs with a linear order on the vertices), where an interval minor is obtained by deleting edges and contracting pairs of consecutive vertices: deciding whether an ordered graph has a $K_t$ interval minor is NP-complete, but the authors give a polynomial-time $f(t)$-approximation algorithm with $f$ triply exponential in $t$, based on delayed decompositions.
notes: Stated in the introduction as a known open problem without a labelled environment and without explicit attribution to specific authors; captured because the authors explicitly flag it as open and use it to motivate the paper.
paper_title: A Polynomial-Time Approximation Algorithm for Complete Interval Minors
